the genetic defect in the regulation and expression of the immune response to (T,G) A-L, as measured by the ability to produce (T,G)- A-L specific T cell help, is present in all SLE patients tested and is not inherited by their first degree relatives who are healthy.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
in contrast to SLE patients the genetic regulation of immune responses was intact in healthy first degree relatives of SLE patients.
the genetic regulation of immune responses to (T,G) -A-L is not altered in SLE patients or their healthy family members.
the ability to respond genetically regulated antigens in the first degree relatives of SLE patients is not impaired.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the immune defect observed in SLE patients is a disease specific phenomenon and not a manifestation of a general defect in the genetic regulation of immune responses.
the genetic defect in SLE patients that results in a general defect in immune regulation, is not a defect in the genetic regulation of immune response potential.
the genetic regulation of immune responses is intact in the healthy relatives of patients with SLE.
